title: Episode 5: Working with Issues
description: Filing, searching, filtering, commenting on, and managing GitHub issues.
concepts: What an issue is: a unit of work, bug report, or feature request
The Issues tab: list view, filters, and search
Issue anatomy: title, body (markdown), labels, assignees, milestone
Filtering issues: by label, author, assignee, milestone, open/closed
Using the search bar with qualifiers like is:open label:bug
Reading an issue: the timeline of comments, events, and references
Filing a new issue: writing a clear title and descriptive body
Using markdown in issue bodies: code blocks, lists, task lists, links
Commenting on issues: adding context, asking questions, reacting
Referencing issues from other issues or pull requests with #number
Assigning an issue to yourself or someone else
Closing an issue and what closed means
The connection between issues and pull requests
Using gh issue commands from the terminal as an alternative
transcriptText:
[ALEX]
Welcome back. Today we're working with one of the most important parts of GitHub: issues.

[JAMIE]
And for a lot of learners, this is where GitHub starts to feel social, right? Not just files and commits, but conversation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Issues are where people report bugs, request features, ask for clarification, track chores, and coordinate work. In open source, a lot of collaboration begins there.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
Before we get into the mechanics, a few support notes matter here. This chapter pairs well with the official GitHub documentation about issues, GitHub's accessibility guide for issues, and the GitHub Accessibility Lab CLI guide. There are also related appendices on advanced search, GitHub Mobile, and a screen reader cheat sheet.

[JAMIE]
So if someone wants the official source of truth, or a companion reference with current product details, those are the places to check.

[ALEX]
Right. And there's an accessibility note that matters especially for screen reader users. This lesson assumes GitHub's improved issues experience, which has better landmark structure and live announcements. Depending on your account, this may already be active automatically.

[JAMIE]
How would someone verify that?

[ALEX]
Open the user menu at the top right of GitHub, go to Feature preview, and look for the New Issues Experience. If it's listed and enabled, you're set. If it's listed and not enabled, turn it on. If it's not listed at all, that usually means it has already become part of the standard interface.

[JAMIE]
And for NVDA users, there's also that constant question: browse mode or focus mode?

[ALEX]
Yes. Use browse mode for reading headings, lists, and issue content. Switch to focus mode when typing in fields like search boxes, title boxes, and comment editors. And remember that NVDA plus F7 is a strong orientation tool because it gives you lists of headings, links, form fields, buttons, and landmarks.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
This chapter is also the first issue-based challenge chapter. The pattern is simple: claim, act, confirm.

[JAMIE]
Meaning first understand where you are and what you're supposed to do, then do the task, then verify the result.

[ALEX]
Exactly. There are two core challenges and one optional extension. First, create your first issue. Second, comment on another issue and use an at-mention. Optional: add a sub-issue if that feature is enabled in your repository.

[JAMIE]
And importantly, no branch work yet.

[ALEX]
Correct. No branch, no file editing, no pull request. This chapter is all issue work. Your evidence is in the issue threads and issue metadata.

[JAMIE]
That's useful because beginners often assume every GitHub action needs a branch.

[ALEX]
Not here. When you complete the challenges, you post evidence in your assigned challenge issues, including the issue numbers you created or commented on, and then you close those assigned challenge issues.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
If you prefer the command line, there are a few good habits to keep in sequence. First, confirm repository context with commands like git remote dash v and gh repo view. Second, read before writing: use gh issue view and understand the issue before you comment or edit. Third, keep comments focused and actionable. Fourth, verify each action from output, such as checking gh issue list dash dash assignee at me. And fifth, stay with documented options from gh help and the manual.

[JAMIE]
I like that. It keeps terminal work from becoming guesswork.

[ALEX]
Yes. Especially for accessibility and reliability.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let's ground this. What is a GitHub issue, really?

[ALEX]
A GitHub issue is a tracked conversation attached to a repository. It has a title, a body, metadata like labels and assignees, a numbered identity such as issue 150, and a timeline of comments and activity.

[JAMIE]
So it's more structured than a chat message.

[ALEX]
Much more. Issues are durable. They can be searched, filtered, referenced, assigned, grouped into milestones, linked to pull requests, and sometimes broken into sub-issues.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
How do you get to the issues list?

[ALEX]
Two common ways. From a repository page, activate the Issues tab in the repository navigation. Or go directly by URL if you know the repository path and append slash issues.

[JAMIE]
And for keyboard users, there are shortcuts too.

[ALEX]
Yes. On GitHub, pressing G then I jumps to issues in many contexts. That can be faster than tabbing through repository navigation.

[JAMIE]
What should a learner expect on the issues list page?

[ALEX]
Think of it as a dashboard of conversations. You'll usually find the page heading, controls for filtering and searching, buttons for open and closed issues, maybe labels or milestone filters, the New issue button, and then the list itself.

[JAMIE]
How should someone read that list with a screen reader?

[ALEX]
Jump by headings if the page is structured that way, or use links and list navigation. Each issue entry usually tells you the title, issue number, whether it's open or closed, who opened it, and sometimes labels, assignees, comments count, or related metadata.

[JAMIE]
So the key skill is not just finding the list, but learning what each row is announcing.

[ALEX]
Exactly. You're listening for enough information to decide whether to open it.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
And once the list gets crowded, filtering becomes the real superpower.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. GitHub gives you a search and filter bar, plus filter controls. You can filter by label, combine filters, filter by milestone, search by keywords, and switch between open and closed issues.

[JAMIE]
Can we make that more concrete?

[ALEX]
Sure. If you want beginner-friendly work, filter by the label good first issue. If you want issues assigned to you, use an assignee filter. If you want a specific planning target, filter by milestone. And if you know a word from the title or description, search with that keyword.

[JAMIE]
And combining filters means narrowing the list with more than one condition at once.

[ALEX]
Right. For example: open issues with a specific label and a specific milestone. That gives you a much smaller, more relevant list.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let's talk terminal. What if someone wants to list their assigned challenge issues from the command line?

[ALEX]
You can use the GitHub CLI to list issues, including filtering for issues assigned to you. A typical pattern is gh issue list with an assignee filter such as at me. The exact flags can vary, so use gh issue list dash dash help when needed.

[JAMIE]
And viewing a specific issue in the terminal?

[ALEX]
That's typically gh issue view followed by the issue number. One of the nice things there is that Markdown renders in the terminal output, so headings, lists, and emphasis are easier to read than raw source.

[JAMIE]
What if the terminal view isn't enough?

[ALEX]
You can open the issue in your browser instead, and there are options to focus on the comments if you only want to read discussion. The principle is the same: choose the view that helps you read effectively.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
So now we've found issues. How do we read one well?

[ALEX]
When you land on an issue page, first orient yourself. Identify the title, the issue number, whether it's open or closed, and the main issue description. Then look at the comment thread and activity timeline.

[JAMIE]
What does quick navigation look like here?

[ALEX]
Use headings, landmarks, or element lists with your screen reader. If you're sighted or low vision, scan for the title at the top, the description body beneath it, and the activity thread below. If you're in the terminal, gh issue view can present the description and comments in a clean sequence.

[JAMIE]
And what specifically should we read in the issue description?

[ALEX]
Look for what happened, what the author expected, how to reproduce the problem if it's a bug, what environment they were using, and any extra context. Even if those exact labels aren't used, those are the core ideas.

[JAMIE]
Then comments tell you how the conversation evolved.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Comments may confirm the problem, ask follow-up questions, suggest fixes, reference related issues or pull requests, or note status changes.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
All right. Let's leave a comment.

[ALEX]
There are two main styles with the GitHub CLI. Interactive mode opens your default editor, usually through the EDITOR environment variable, so you can write the comment there. Inline mode lets you provide the comment text directly on the command line.

[JAMIE]
And in the browser?

[ALEX]
Open the issue, move to the comment box at the bottom, type your message, and activate Comment. On many GitHub pages, Control plus Enter submits the comment.

[JAMIE]
What about Markdown while typing?

[ALEX]
GitHub comments support Markdown, so you can use plain paragraphs, lists, inline code, links, and emphasis. But for issue comments, clarity matters more than decoration. Keep it focused.

[JAMIE]
And helpful.

[ALEX]
Yes. A useful comment might confirm a bug, clarify reproduction steps, suggest a location in the repository, or offer a next action.

[JAMIE]
This is where at-mentions come in, right?

[ALEX]
Exactly. Typing at followed by a username notifies that person. It's a direct way to bring someone into the conversation.

[JAMIE]
So if I comment, "At classmate, I can confirm the link is broken," GitHub alerts them.

[ALEX]
That's right. And that's why the chapter's second challenge includes an at-mention. It teaches the communication pattern, not just the typing pattern.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can we walk through that challenge clearly?

[ALEX]
Yes. Open your Learning Room repository's Issues tab. Find an issue created by another student, or a facilitator-provided practice issue. Open it and read the description first. Then go to the comment box. Write a helpful comment that includes an at-mention of the issue author. For example, you might confirm the problem, correct a shortcut, or suggest where new text should go. Then submit the comment.

[JAMIE]
And you're done when the comment appears in the thread and the username renders as a link.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Now let's file a new issue.

[ALEX]
From the repository's Issues page, activate New issue. Some repositories show a template picker first. If so, choose a suitable template, or open a blank issue if that's what the challenge calls for.

[JAMIE]
Then we fill out the form.

[ALEX]
Right. The most common pieces are the title and the description body. The title should be specific. Not "Problem" or "Help." Instead, something like "Keyboard shortcuts table has incorrect NVDA modifier key" or "Setup guide link to accessibility settings is broken."

[JAMIE]
So the title should help someone understand the issue before opening it.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Then in the body, explain what happened, what you expected, how to reproduce it if relevant, your environment, and any additional context.

[JAMIE]
Let's unpack those.

[ALEX]
What happened means the actual behavior or problem. What I expected means the correct or desired behavior. How to reproduce means the exact steps someone else can follow to observe the same issue. Environment includes things like browser, operating system, device, screen reader, zoom level, or other tools involved. Additional context is anything else that makes the report more understandable.

[JAMIE]
And labels can be assigned from the sidebar if you have permission.

[ALEX]
Yes. Labels help classify the issue. Then you submit it.

[JAMIE]
What about the CLI version of filing an issue?

[ALEX]
There are two broad approaches. Interactive mode prompts you for title, body, labels, and assignees. Inline mode lets you provide those values directly on the command line. And if the repository has issue templates, you may be able to use one of those templates rather than starting from scratch.

[JAMIE]
So browser and CLI both support structured issue creation, just with different interaction styles.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Can we go through the first challenge step by step?

[ALEX]
Yes. Open your Learning Room repository. Go to Issues, either through the tab or with G then I. Activate New issue. If a template picker appears, choose Open a blank issue unless a template clearly fits. In the title field, enter a clear title of at least about a dozen characters. In the body, write a meaningful description of at least around eighty characters. Include what the problem is, where it is in the repository, and what fix you think should happen. Then submit the issue and save the issue number or URL.

[JAMIE]
And the chapter frames this as an "agentic strategy" too.

[ALEX]
Yes. A clear issue is not only useful for humans. It is also a strong prompt for an AI agent. If you describe an accessibility problem or content chore clearly, you make it easier for a person or a tool to act on it.

[JAMIE]
That's a great bridge between accessibility, open source, and AI workflows.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
What about cross-referencing issues?

[ALEX]
Very important. You can mention another issue in a comment by typing its number or a full reference. In many contexts, GitHub turns that into a link.

[JAMIE]
And there are also closing keywords.

[ALEX]
Yes. In pull request descriptions, and sometimes in issue comments depending on context, keywords like closes, fixes, or resolves followed by an issue reference can automatically close the linked issue when the pull request is merged.

[JAMIE]
That's useful because it connects discussion to implementation.

[ALEX]
Exactly. And cross-repo references let you point to an issue in another repository when work spans projects.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Now the optional extension: sub-issues.

[ALEX]
Sub-issues let you break a larger issue into smaller, trackable child issues. The parent issue can show progress as those child issues are completed.

[JAMIE]
When should someone use sub-issues?

[ALEX]
When a problem is too large to track as one step. For example, "Fix accessibility in welcome dot md" might be split into "Add alt text," "Fix heading hierarchy," and "Correct link text."

[JAMIE]
How do you create one?

[ALEX]
Open the parent issue. Look for a Sub-issues section, an Add sub-issue button, or a Create sub-issue option. Create a new sub-issue with a clear title and short description. Once created, it appears nested under the parent.

[JAMIE]
And when you're reading a parent issue, you can see its child issues there.

[ALEX]
Right. And when you read a child issue, GitHub may show its parent relationship too.

[JAMIE]
How is that different from a task list?

[ALEX]
A task list is lighter weight, usually just checkboxes in issue text. Sub-issues are full issues with their own pages, metadata, discussion, and tracking. Use task lists for simple checkboxes; use sub-issues when each piece deserves independent conversation and status.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let's shift into maintainer and triager skills. What does managing issues include?

[ALEX]
Closing and reopening issues, assigning them, changing labels, setting milestones, and sometimes transferring or deleting issues if you have the necessary permissions.

[JAMIE]
Closing sounds simple, but there are nuances.

[ALEX]
Yes. You can close an issue directly. In some workflows you may specify a reason, such as completed or not planned. You may also close with a comment so the author understands why. And if closure was premature, you can reopen the issue.

[JAMIE]
And assigning means identifying who will work on it.

[ALEX]
Correct. You might assign yourself, add or remove labels, or set a milestone to place the issue in a release or project target.

[JAMIE]
What about changing labels?

[ALEX]
Labels aren't fixed forever. As understanding improves, an issue may move from question to bug, or from general to accessibility, or gain a priority label. Updating labels is part of triage.

[JAMIE]
And transferring or deleting an issue?

[ALEX]
Those are more advanced administrative actions. Transfer is for when the issue belongs in another repository. Deletion is rare and usually reserved for spam or mistakes, depending on project policy.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let's talk about one special label: good first issue.

[ALEX]
That label is often your entry point into open source. It signals work that's considered approachable for newcomers.

[JAMIE]
So if I'm overwhelmed by a huge issues list, good first issue gives me a starting lane.

[ALEX]
Exactly. It doesn't guarantee trivial work, but it usually means the maintainers think the task is suitable for someone getting started.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Now I really want to spend time on accessibility-specific issue writing, because this audience needs that.

[ALEX]
Absolutely. An accessibility issue should be concrete, reproducible, and respectful. Say what assistive technology or visual setting you used. Describe what happened, what you expected, how someone can reproduce it, the environment, and any additional context.

[JAMIE]
So not just "screen reader broken."

[ALEX]
Exactly. Better would be something like: when navigating to the keyboard shortcuts table with NVDA and Firefox, the modifier key is described incorrectly. Expected behavior: the table should identify Insert or Caps Lock as the NVDA key. Reproduction steps: open the page, jump to the shortcuts table, read the NVDA row. Environment: Windows, Firefox, NVDA version such-and-such. Additional context: the incorrect instruction may mislead new users.

[JAMIE]
That's much more actionable.

[ALEX]
Yes. A well-filed accessibility issue respects both the user impact and the maintainer's need for clear evidence.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
That leads naturally to writing effective issues in general.

[ALEX]
Right. For bug reports, you usually want a clear problem statement, expected behavior, reproduction steps, environment, and context. For feature requests, explain the need, who benefits, what outcome you want, and any constraints or examples. For all issue types, write specifically, keep the scope clear, and avoid vague titles and vague bodies.

[JAMIE]
Can you give the before-and-after pattern?

[ALEX]
Sure. A vague issue might be titled "Accessibility problem" with a body like "This page is hard to use." A clearer issue would say exactly which page, exactly what failed, exactly how to reproduce it, and exactly what should change.

[JAMIE]
So effective issues lower the cognitive load for the next person.

[ALEX]
Exactly. They reduce back-and-forth and increase the chance of a useful response.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
What about navigating these workflows accessibly in practice? The source had some practical notes.

[ALEX]
Yes. For screen reader users, it helps to verify page structure quickly. For example, on a new issue page, the title field should be one of the first major form controls. If you use heading navigation, confirm the first heading matches the task you're doing. On the issues list, moving by heading level can be faster than arrowing through every element. If a template picker appears, tab and enter are often the fastest way to choose Open a blank issue.

[JAMIE]
And for low-vision users?

[ALEX]
The New issue button is usually prominent and remains visible even at high zoom. The title field is typically full width and easy to locate. The body field expands as you type. After submitting, verify that your title and description rendered correctly on the issue page.

[JAMIE]
And for sighted learners?

[ALEX]
You'll often see the new issue appear near the top of the list with an Open badge. Notice that the issue number is automatically assigned and appears in the URL and page title. That number matters later for cross-references and evidence.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Now let's cover the local Git alternative, because the heading list calls that out.

[ALEX]
Good catch. Working from your local clone doesn't replace GitHub issues, but it can support your issue workflow. From your clone, you can confirm which repository you're connected to with git remote dash v, then use gh repo view and gh issue commands in the terminal without having to navigate entirely in the browser. This is especially useful if you prefer the command line for reading, listing, and posting comments while keeping the repository context grounded in your local checkout.

[JAMIE]
So local Git gives you context, and GitHub CLI gives you issue operations.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Let's make sure we cover the command-focused mini tasks clearly: list assigned challenge issues, view a specific issue in the terminal, leave a comment, and create a new issue interactively.

[ALEX]
Right. To list assigned issues, use gh issue list with an assignee filter such as at me. To view a specific issue in the terminal, use gh issue view followed by the issue number. To leave a comment, use the issue comment workflow either interactively through your editor or inline with direct text. To create a new issue interactively, use the issue create workflow so GitHub CLI prompts you for the title and body and, where supported, labels and assignees.

[JAMIE]
And always verify the result after each command.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Read the output. Confirm the issue number. Confirm that the comment posted. Confirm the repository context.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
What are the expected outcomes for this chapter?

[ALEX]
By the end, you should be able to explain what an issue is, navigate to the issues list, read issue metadata, filter and search issues, open and understand an issue thread, leave a useful comment, create a clear new issue, use an at-mention, understand cross-references, recognize when sub-issues are appropriate, and understand the basics of maintainer triage actions.

[JAMIE]
And for the workshop specifically, you should have completed the challenge actions and posted evidence.

[ALEX]
Yes. Your evidence comment should say that Chapter 5 is completed and list the issue numbers for Challenge 2, Challenge 3, and the optional sub-issue if you did it. Then you close your assigned challenge issues.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
If someone gets stuck, what's the healthiest next move?

[ALEX]
Pause and simplify. Confirm you're in the right repository. Read the issue or form before acting. Use GitHub's page structure tools like headings and landmarks, or the CLI help output. Ask a facilitator or classmate for orientation help, especially if the interface differs from the lesson. And remember: if a repository uses templates, that's a support feature, not an obstacle.

[JAMIE]
That feels important. Getting stuck in issues often isn't about understanding the concept. It's about orientation.

[ALEX]
Exactly.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Was there a broader learning moment in this chapter?

[ALEX]
Yes. Today, you are doing triage manually. That matters because later you may use automation or AI agents for issue tracking, prioritization, or first-response workflows. But if you don't know how to read, file, comment on, label, and understand issues yourself, you won't be able to judge whether an automated system is helping or making mistakes.

[JAMIE]
So manual issue work is the foundation. Automation is the amplifier.

[ALEX]
Perfectly said.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
And the learning pattern here really is that same claim, act, confirm loop.

[ALEX]
Yes. Claim the task and context. Act by filing, commenting, or organizing. Confirm by checking the output, issue number, visible metadata, or posted comment.

[JAMIE]
That pattern is small, but it scales.

[ALEX]
It does. It works for web workflows, terminal workflows, and accessible workflows.

[PAUSE]
[JAMIE]
Before we wrap, I want to circle back to one simple but powerful idea: issues are not just for reporting errors.

[ALEX]
Right. They're for bugs, features, chores, documentation gaps, accessibility problems, planning, decomposition into sub-issues, and collaboration. If a repository has work to discuss and track, issues are often where that happens.

[JAMIE]
And if you're new to open source, the issues list is often the map.

[ALEX]
Exactly. Especially when you use filters like good first issue and read carefully before jumping in.

[PAUSE]
[ALEX]
So your practical next step is simple: go complete the issue challenges. File your first clear issue. Read someone else's issue carefully. Leave a helpful comment with an at-mention. If your repository supports it, try adding a sub-issue. Then post your evidence and verify that everything appears as expected.

[JAMIE]
And once you can do that confidently, you're ready for the next layer of GitHub collaboration.

[ALEX]
You are. Nice work.

# Working with Issues
>
> **Listen to Episode 5:** [Working with Issues](https://lp.csedesigns.com/ggg/PODCASTS.html) - a conversational audio overview of this chapter. Listen before reading to preview the concepts, or after to reinforce what you learned.

> **Related appendices:** [Appendix N: Advanced Search](appendix-n-advanced-search.md) | [Appendix V: GitHub Mobile](appendix-v-github-mobile.md) | [Appendix B: Screen Reader Cheat Sheet](appendix-b-screen-reader-cheatsheet.md)
> **Authoritative sources:** [GitHub Docs: About issues](https://docs.github.com/en/issues/tracking-your-work-with-issues/about-issues) | [GitHub Accessibility Guide: Issues](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/issues/) | [GitHub Accessibility Lab: CLI Guide](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/cli/)

## Filing, Managing, and Participating in GitHub Issues

> Issues are where open source collaboration begins. This guide covers everything from finding the right issue to file a perfect bug report - all with your keyboard and screen reader.
>
> **Official GitHub Accessibility Guide:** GitHub publishes an NVDA-focused guide for working with issues using a screen reader at [Using GitHub Issues with a Screen Reader](https://accessibility.github.com/documentation/guide/issues/). This chapter covers the same material with additional perspectives (VoiceOver, low vision, CLI) and workshop-specific challenges. Use the official guide as a companion reference.
>
> **Screen reader note - New Issues Experience:** This guide uses GitHub's improved Issues experience, which provides better ARIA landmark structure and live-region announcements for screen readers. This feature may already be active for your account - it has been broadly rolled out and may no longer appear as a Feature Preview toggle at all.
>
> **To verify:** Activate the **User Menu** button (top-right of any GitHub page) → activate **"Feature preview"** → scan the list for **"New Issues Experience"**:
>
> - If listed and the toggle announces **"Pressed"** (or **"Disable"**) - already enabled, no action needed
> - If listed but **not Pressed** (or **"Enable"**) - activate the toggle to enable it
> - If not listed at all - the feature has graduated to the standard interface; it is active automatically
>
> Full step-by-step instructions with per-screen-reader commands are in [Pre-Workshop Setup, Step 4](00-pre-workshop-setup.md#step-4---check-github-feature-preview-settings).
>
> **Browse vs Focus Mode (NVDA):** Toggle between modes with `NVDA+Space` (NVDA key = `Insert` or `Caps Lock`). Use **Browse Mode** (the default) for reading lists, headings, and issue content. Switch to **Focus Mode** when typing in text fields and search boxes. Use `NVDA+F7` at any time to open a list of all headings, links, form fields, buttons, and landmarks on the page - this is your orientation tool.

## Workshop Recommendation (Chapter 5 / Challenges 2-3)

Chapter 5 is the first **issue-based challenge chapter** with short, confidence-building tasks. It supports Challenge 2 (File Your First Issue) and Challenge 3 (Join the Conversation).

- **Challenge count:** 2 core challenges plus one optional extension
- **Time per challenge:** under 10 minutes
- **Evidence:** issue comments and issue metadata
- **Pattern:** claim -> act -> confirm

### CLI getting-started principles for issue work

If you prefer terminal workflows, keep this sequence:

1. Confirm repository context first (`git remote -v` and `gh repo view`).
2. Read before writing (`gh issue view <number>` before commenting or editing).
3. Keep comments focused, specific, and actionable.
4. Verify each action from output (`gh issue list --assignee @me`).
5. Use only documented options from `gh --help` and the manual.

### Chapter 5 Challenge Set

1. **Create your first issue** - file a new issue with a clear title and description.
2. **Comment and @mention** - leave a comment on a classmate's issue and tag them with an @mention.
3. **Optional extension: Add a sub-issue** - break a larger issue into smaller, trackable pieces if your repository has sub-issues enabled.

> **Branch guidance for Chapter 5:** Chapter 5 focuses on issue skills. You do NOT need to create a branch or edit any files for these challenges. All your work happens in GitHub issue threads. File editing and branches start in Chapter 6.
>
> **How completion works:** When you finish the issue challenges, post evidence in your assigned challenge issues with links to the issue you created and the comment you posted. The facilitator reviews your issue activity directly. No pull request is required for Chapter 5.

### Challenge 2 Step-by-Step: Create Your First Issue

**Goal:** File a new issue in your Learning Room repository with a specific title and a meaningful description.

> **Agentic strategy:** Issues are the prompts that wake up AI. A clear issue for a human is also a prompt for an agent. For this challenge, log an issue describing an accessibility problem or chore you wish an AI agent could fix for you.

**Where you are working:** the Issues tab of your Learning Room repository on GitHub.com.

1. Open your Learning Room repository in your browser.

## What Is a GitHub Issue?

An issue is a discussion thread attached to a repository. Issues are used for:

- **Bug reports** - "This feature doesn't work when using a screen reader"
- **Feature requests** - "It would help if the submit button had an accessible label"
- **Questions** - "How do I configure X for Y use case?"
- **Tasks** - "Update the README with screen reader instructions"
- **Accessibility reports** - "The infinite scroll carousel is not keyboard accessible"

Every issue has a **number** (`#42`), a **state** (Open or Closed), a **title**, a **description**, and a **comment thread**. Issues are public by default on public repositories.

> **Learning Room connection:** In your Learning Room repo, every challenge from `docs/CHALLENGES.md` becomes an issue. For example, Challenge 1 ("Fix Broken Link") is filed as an issue pointing to `docs/welcome.md`, describing the broken link and linking to the challenge success criteria. When you open a PR to fix it, you reference the issue with `Closes #XX` to automatically close it on merge.

## Cross-Referencing Issues

Linking issues and PRs to each other creates a trail of context that helps everyone understand the project's history.

### Closing keywords in PR descriptions or issue comments

When you type these phrases in a PR description or comment (followed by an issue number), GitHub creates a connection:

| Keyword | Effect on merge |
| ---------  | ----------------  |
| `Closes #42` | Closes issue #42 when the PR merges |
| `Fixes #42` | Same - typically for bugs |
| `Resolves #42` | Same - general use |
| `refs #42` | Creates a reference without auto-closing |
| `cc @username` | Notifies the person |

### Mentioning another issue in a comment

Simply type `#` followed by a number anywhere in a comment body. GitHub autocompletes with a dropdown of matching issues and PRs:

```text
Step 1: Type # in the comment box (Focus Mode)
Step 2: A dropdown appears with issues and PRs
Step 3: ↑/↓ to navigate, or type more numbers to filter
Step 4: Enter to insert the reference
```

### Cross-repo references

`owner/repo#42` - references issue #42 in a different repository.

## Sub-Issues - Parent and Child Relationships

**Sub-issues** (released 2025) let you nest issues inside a parent issue to break large work into tracked pieces. A "parent" issue contains a list of child issues; each child is a full issue with its own discussion, labels, and assignees.

### When to Use Sub-Issues

| Use case | Example |
| ----------  | ---------  |
| Large feature broken down | Parent: "Redesign navigation"; Children: "Keyboard nav," "Screen reader nav," "Mobile nav" |
| Epic tracking | Parent: "WCAG 2.1 AA compliance"; Children: one issue per failing criterion |
| Release milestone | Parent: "v2.0 release"; Children: every required PR/fix |

```text

2. Scroll to (or H-navigate to) the "Sub-issues" section in the issue body/sidebar
3. Tab to "Add sub-issue" button → Enter
4. Type the issue number or title to search
5. Select the issue from the dropdown → Enter to link
   Or: select "Create new issue" to create and link in one step
```

**Screen reader note:** The sub-issues section is announced as a region. After linking, the child issue appears as a list item with a checkbox showing its open/closed state. Tab through to read each child's title and status.

```text

↓ → list of linked child issues
Each item: [checkbox state] [issue title] [#number] [open/closed badge]

```

**Progress indicator:** The parent issue shows a completion bar (e.g., "3 of 7 completed") based on how many child issues are closed. Screen readers announce this as a progress region.

Every child issue shows a "Parent issue" link near the top of the page (above the description). Navigate with `H` or links (`K`) to find it.

### Sub-Issues vs. Task Lists

| Feature | Task list checkboxes | Sub-issues |
| ---------  | ---------------------  | ------------  |
| Location | Issue description (Markdown) | Sidebar/section (structured data) |
| Each item is | Text line + checkbox | A full GitHub issue |
| Tracked in Projects | No (checkbox only) | Yes (each child tracks independently) |
| Cross-repo | No | Yes |
| Best for | Quick checklists in one issue | Multi-issue work tracking |

> **Workshop tip:** If you are working on a feature that requires multiple PRs or involves several team members, ask the maintainer to create a parent issue. You can then claim individual child issues without one person owning the whole feature.

## Accessibility-Specific Issue Writing Tips

When filing accessibility bugs, these details help maintainers reproduce and fix the problem:

1. **Screen reader and version** - "NVDA 2025.3.3" not just "screen reader"
2. **OS and version** - "Windows 11 22H2"
3. **Browser and version** - "Chrome 124.0.6367.82"
4. **GitHub interface** - "Modern experience (default since Jan 2026)" or "Classic experience (opted out)"
5. **What was announced** - quote the exact text your screen reader spoke
6. **What should have been announced** - describe the expected behavior
7. **ARIA issue if known** - e.g., "The button has no accessible name"
8. **Steps to reproduce** - numbered, step-by-step
9. **Frequency** - "This happens every time" vs "intermittent"

After filtering, the screen reader should announce something like

## How to reproduce
1. Navigate to any repo's Issues tab
2. Press B to navigate to the "Label" filter button
3. Press Enter to open the dropdown
4. Select the "accessibility" label
5. Press Escape to close
6. Notice: no announcement that filtering has been applied

## Environment
- Screen reader: NVDA 2025.3.3 (with NVDA+Chrome)
- Browser: Chrome 124.0.6367.82
- OS: Windows 11 22H2
- GitHub interface: Modern experience (default since Jan 2026)

- Include your screen reader name and version (e.g., "NVDA 2025.3.3") plus browser and OS; this lets maintainers reproduce with the same toolchain
- Test with a second screen reader or browser if possible and note the results -- "Also fails in JAWS 2026 with Chrome; works in VoiceOver with Safari" dramatically narrows the debugging scope

## Writing Effective Issues

> **See also:** [Appendix N: Advanced Search](appendix-n-advanced-search.md) covers search qualifiers to find existing issues before filing a new one.

A well-written issue saves everyone time -- the maintainer who reads it, the contributor who fixes it, and the future searcher who finds it six months later. This section gives you reusable templates for the two most common issue types and a set of principles that apply to every issue you file.

### Bug Report Structure

A strong bug report answers five questions. Use this template every time you report something broken.

| Section | What to write |
|---|---|
| **Title** | Follow the formula: "When I [action], [unexpected result] instead of [expected result]" |
| **Steps to Reproduce** | Numbered list -- start from the earliest relevant step |
| **Expected Behavior** | What *should* happen according to documentation or common sense |
| **Actual Behavior** | What *does* happen -- include exact error messages or screenshots |
| **Environment** | OS, browser, screen reader, app version -- anything that might matter |

The title formula is the most important part. A title like "When I press Enter on the Submit button, nothing happens instead of creating the issue" tells the maintainer exactly what is broken before they even open the issue.

> **Screen reader tip:** When pasting error messages into the Actual Behavior section, wrap them in a fenced code block (triple backticks). Screen readers will announce "code block" so the listener knows the text is a literal error, not your description.

**Steps to Reproduce matter more than you think.** Maintainers cannot fix what they cannot recreate. Number every step, starting from a clean slate -- "Open the repository" is better than "Go to the page." Include what you clicked, what keyboard shortcut you pressed, and what happened after each step.

### Feature Request Structure

Feature requests work best when they focus on the *problem* before jumping to the solution. Use this four-part structure:

1. **Problem statement** -- Describe the pain point. What are you trying to do, and why is it hard or impossible right now?
2. **Proposed solution** -- Your best idea for fixing the problem. Be specific enough to discuss, but hold it loosely.
3. **Alternatives considered** -- Other approaches you thought about and why they fell short. This shows you have done your homework.
4. **Who benefits** -- Name the audience. "Screen reader users navigating large repositories" is more compelling than "everyone."

A feature request that starts with "I want a dark mode toggle" is weaker than one that starts with "Low-vision users report eyestrain after 20 minutes because the current theme has insufficient contrast." The second version gives maintainers something to design around.

### General Issue Writing Principles

These rules apply to every issue -- bugs, features, questions, and everything in between.

**One issue per problem.** If you discovered two bugs during the same session, file two separate issues. Combining them makes it impossible to close one without the other and clutters the conversation.

**Write searchable titles.** Future contributors will search before filing. "Bug with button" will never surface in a search for "Submit button unresponsive on Safari." Front-load the title with the specific component or action.

**Include context, not assumptions.** Instead of "The API is broken," write "The `/repos` endpoint returns a 403 when I pass a valid token." Let maintainers draw their own conclusions from the evidence you provide.

**Link related issues.** If your bug might be connected to issue #42, mention it: "This might be related to #42." GitHub automatically creates a back-link, building a web of context that helps everyone. You will learn more about cross-referencing in [Chapter 6](06-working-with-pull-requests.md).

| Principle | Bad example | Good example |
|---|---|---|
| One issue per problem | "The button is broken and also the logo is wrong" | Two separate issues, each with its own title |
| Searchable title | "Help needed" | "Keyboard focus lost after closing modal dialog" |
| Context over assumptions | "Nothing works" | "After upgrading to v2.3, the dashboard returns a blank page on Firefox 124" |
| Link related issues | (no mention) | "Possibly related to #42 -- same component, different trigger" |

### Before and After: A Vague Issue vs. a Clear Issue

**Vague issue (hard to act on):**

> **Title:** Bug
>
> It doesn't work. I tried clicking and nothing happened. Please fix.

The maintainer has to ask: What doesn't work? Where did you click? What browser? What did you expect? Every follow-up question costs a round-trip of waiting.

**Clear issue (ready to fix):**

> **Title:** When I press Enter on the "New issue" button, nothing happens instead of opening the issue form
>
> **Steps to Reproduce:**
>
> 1. Navigate to github.com/org/repo
> 2. Press `G` then `I` to go to the Issues tab
> 3. Tab to the "New issue" button
> 4. Press `Enter`
>
> **Expected:** The new issue form opens.
>
> **Actual:** The page does not respond. No error in the console.
>
> **Environment:** Windows 11, Firefox 128, JAWS 2025

The maintainer can reproduce this in under a minute. No follow-up questions needed -- the fix can start immediately.

> **Screen reader tip:** You can use the issue template feature in GitHub to pre-fill these sections automatically. If the repository provides templates, your screen reader will announce each section heading as you Tab through the form. You will set up your own issue templates in [Chapter 17](17-issue-templates.md).

### Learning Cards: Writing Effective Issues

<details>
<summary>Screen reader users</summary>

- Use fenced code blocks (triple backticks) when pasting error messages or screen reader output; your screen reader announces "code block" so listeners know the text is literal, not description
- When writing "Steps to Reproduce," type each step as a numbered Markdown list item (`1.`, `2.`, etc.) so screen readers announce "list with N items"
- Type `#` in the comment body to trigger issue autocomplete; press `Down Arrow` to navigate matching issues and `Enter` to insert a cross-reference link

</details>

<details>
<summary>Low vision users</summary>

- Use the Preview tab (next to Write) to check your Markdown rendering before submitting; headings, bold text, and code blocks are much easier to proofread in rendered form
- Screenshots with alt text are valuable evidence; add them with the image button in the formatting toolbar or drag-and-drop into the body field
- Keep paragraphs short (3-4 sentences max) so the issue is scannable at high zoom without excessive scrolling

</details>

<details>
<summary>Sighted users</summary>

- A well-structured issue uses H2 headings (##) for major sections: What happened, Expected, How to reproduce, Environment
- GitHub renders Markdown tables in issue bodies; use a table to compare expected vs. actual behavior side by side
- The title appears in issue lists, email notifications, and search results; front-load it with the specific component or action for discoverability

</details>

## Try It: File Your First Issue

**Time:** 3 minutes | **What you need:** Browser, signed in to GitHub

Go to the Learning Room repository and file a real issue:

1. Navigate to the Issues tab (press `G` then `I` in Focus Mode)
2. Find and activate the "New issue" button (`K` to links, or `Tab` to it)
3. In the title field, type: **"Introduce myself - [Your Name]"**
4. In the description, write 2-3 sentences: who you are, what screen reader you use, and one thing you're hoping to learn today
5. Press `Ctrl+Enter` to submit (or Tab to the Submit button and press `Enter`)

**You're done.** You just filed your first GitHub issue. Go read someone else's introduction and leave a friendly comment - press `3` to jump between issue titles on the Issues list.

> **What success feels like:** Your issue is live. Other participants can see it. You just contributed to a real repository - and it took less than three minutes.

### Learning Cards: Filing Your First Issue

**Screen reader users:**

- After pressing `Ctrl+Enter` to submit, listen for the page reload; GitHub navigates to your new issue page where the title is the first heading -- press `1` to confirm it matches what you typed
- Navigate the issue list with `3` (heading level 3) to jump between issue titles; this is faster than arrowing through every element on the page
- If the template picker appears, use `Tab` and `Enter` to select "Open a blank issue"; template names are announced as link text

**Low-vision users:**

- The "New issue" button is prominent and green on the Issues list page; at high zoom it remains visible near the top of the page and does not collapse into a menu
- The title field is full-width and the body field expands as you type; both are easy to locate and target at any zoom level
- After submitting, your new issue page shows your avatar, title, and description in high-contrast-friendly layout; verify the content rendered correctly before moving on

**Sighted users:**

- Your issue immediately appears at the top of the Issues list; the green "Open" badge confirms it was created successfully
- Read a few other students' introduction issues and leave a comment to practice the commenting workflow from the Leaving a Comment section
- Notice how the issue number (e.g., #150) is auto-assigned and appears in the URL and page title; you will use this number for cross-references later

> ### Day 2 Amplifier - Accessibility Agents: `@issue-tracker`
>
> **File, read, comment on, and triage real issues manually before using any agent.** If you have not done the triage work yourself - reading descriptions, assigning labels, identifying duplicates - you cannot evaluate whether an agent's priority scoring is correct. The skill must exist before the amplifier is useful.
>
> Once you have mastered manual issue management:
>
> - **In VS Code** - `@issue-tracker find open issues labeled good-first-issue` searches cross-repository with community sentiment scoring, release-awareness prioritization, and batch-reply capability across every repo you have access to
> - **In your repo** - The issue templates in `accessibility-agents/.github/ISSUE_TEMPLATE/` structure both human filing and automated triage; fork [accessibility-agents](https://github.com/Community-Access/accessibility-agents) and that structure travels into any project you lead
> - **In the cloud** - GitHub Agentic Workflows triage new issues the moment they are opened: applying labels, posting first-response comments, adding to Project boards - the same triage actions you practiced manually today, running at scale
>
> *Today you are the triage engine. On Day 2, you understand the engine well enough to direct it.*
